content: 1. In many regions, the legal, political, economic, and social environments continue to create significant barriers to accessing healthcare and other essential services. 2. In some of these contexts, self-care may represent the only viable option for individuals. A harm-reduction approach is critical in these settings to guide supportive public health strategies and minimize risks to users. 3. Lessons learned from existing implementation efforts can inform future strategies to ensure they are grounded in human rights and are gender-responsive. 4. High-quality health services and self-care interventions must be made available, accessible, affordable, and acceptable to underserved and marginalized populations. This should be based on principles of medical ethics, avoidance of stigma, coercion, and violence, non-discrimination, and the right to health. 5. However, introducing or expanding self-care interventions carries potential risks, such as exacerbating vulnerabilities by shifting government responsibility for quality health services. 6. Transferring control to individuals may inadvertently increase financial burdens and out-of-pocket expenses. 7. Self-care should not be promoted as a cost-saving measure for health systems by shifting costs to users. For example, if users must purchase test kits or supplies that would otherwise be covered by the health system, these costs should remain the responsibility of the health system. 8. The United Nations resolution on Universal Health Coverage (UHC) emphasizes that all individuals should have access to essential health services without discrimination or financial hardship, with a focus on the poor, underserved, and marginalized populations. 9. UHC aspires to ensure equitable access to quality health services without financial hardship, reflecting universal social values such as human security, social cohesion, and solidarity. 10. The WHO UHC Compendium, released in 2020, provides a global repository of health services and interventions to assist countries in progressing toward UHC. 11. Economic considerations are particularly important for underserved populations who may not frequently engage with the health system. Assessing the societal value of self-care interventions, including costs and potential savings for individuals, is critical. 12. Financing models for self-care interventions may need to include government subsidies, private financing, insurance coverage, and partial out-of-pocket payments, adhering to the principle of progressive universalism. 13. Self-care interventions should be integrated into health systems to ensure safety, effectiveness, and diagnostic accuracy, with health worker involvement along the continuum of care. 14. Health systems must identify users requiring varying levels of support to improve access and ensure efficient resource allocation. 15. Self-care, when integrated into health systems, can contribute to better health outcomes by allowing individuals to manage their own care while focusing system resources on those in greater need. 16. Financing distinctions should be made between entirely self-initiated/self-administered tools and those integrated within healthcare provision. 17. Health systems remain accountable for patient outcomes linked to self-care interventions and must monitor the economic and financial implications for households and governments. 18. Community health workers (CHWs) play a critical role in promoting and supporting self-care interventions, reducing inequities in access to care. 19. CHWs require appropriate pre-service education and ongoing training to ensure high-quality service delivery and to address the social, economic, and geographical circumstances of their communities. 20. Respectful, non-judgmental, and non-discriminatory attitudes among health workers are essential for the effective introduction of self-care interventions. 21. Interdisciplinary approaches and inter-professional teamwork can optimize skill mixes and task-sharing, recognizing users as co-producers of their own health. 22. Countries should consider implementing and strengthening the rational delegation of tasks to individuals, caregivers, and communities to achieve equitable health outcomes. 23. Empowering self-carers and caregivers to manage certain aspects of healthcare, under the responsibility of health workers, can enhance the effectiveness of self-care interventions within supportive health systems. 24. The WHO supports the redistribution of specific tasks from highly qualified health workers to those with shorter training, such as CHWs, to optimize the use of available human resources for health.
